passage:
Hi Irawati,
Can I tell you something slightly embarrassing? Last night Harsh showed me a video of Mrinal from his design team presenting her project. He watched it twice and said, "She's so sharp. She makes it look effortless."
I smiled and said, "Wow." Then I went quiet for the rest of dinner.
It's not that I think he likes her. I honestly don't. It's that I heard "sharp" and "effortless" and immediately thought: he has never said that about me. You know I'm the girl who used to compare report cards with the whole class. I started listing everything Mrinal is that I'm not: confident, quick, brilliant with slides. By the time I got home I felt about two inches tall.
So maybe this isn't really about Harsh at all? Does that make sense, or am I being silly?
Ritu

qa.q: What did Harsh say after watching the video of Mrinal twice?
qa.a: He said, "She's so sharp. She makes it look effortless."

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during the rest of dinner?
qa.a: She felt small and jealous, not because she suspected a romance but because the praise made her compare herself with Mrinal and come up short.

qa.q: What could help Ritu at this early stage of comparison?
qa.a: Noticing, as the email begins to, that the feeling is about measuring herself, and perhaps telling Harsh gently that the praise stung, instead of listing Mrinal's strengths.

qa.q: How might Harsh have meant his comment about Mrinal?
qa.a: Harsh was probably just admiring a colleague's work, unaware that his words left Ritu measuring herself against Mrinal.

grounding: Shows a young woman who hears her partner praise a colleague's talent and feels small, because her jealousy is really a comparison with herself.

passage: My friends keep saying, "Zeenat, being Saurabh's girlfriend has turned you into a detective," and they're right, and I hate it. Take Friday. He took forty minutes to reply. Forty. In my head he was with someone. Turns out he was at his cousin's and his phone was in the car. Then on Sunday he liked a photo posted by a girl from his old college, just a picture of her dog, and I stared at that little heart for an hour. When he went out with his friends on Tuesday, I checked who else was tagged. Nobody. And instead of feeling relieved, I thought, maybe he's hiding it better. You see what I mean? He texts good morning every single day. He called me when my exam went badly. I don't count any of that. I only count the forty minutes. It's like my brain has a filter, and it only lets the scary things through.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh take forty minutes to reply on Friday?
qa.a: He was at his cousin's and his phone was in the car.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat stare at the little heart for an hour?
qa.a: Zeenat feels suspicious and anxious, so an ordinary like on a photo of a dog becomes possible evidence in her mind.

qa.q: What could Zeenat try at this stage to get past the filter?
qa.a: She could deliberately list the ordinary facts as well, like his daily good-morning texts and the call after her exam, and pause before reading a slow reply as proof.

qa.q: What might Saurabh be experiencing while Zeenat keeps searching for evidence?
qa.a: Saurabh seems to be behaving as usual, texting every morning, and is probably unaware that his slow replies and likes are being weighed as proof.

grounding: Shows a young woman reading a slow reply, a like and a night out as evidence while ignoring the many ordinary facts against her fear.

passage: Looking back at last spring, I can see how, as Adil's girlfriend, I tested him like a science experiment, except I never learned anything. I'd say, half joking, "Go on, have fun with your gang, I'm sure everyone will be thrilled you're single for the night." Then I'd watch his face. Some days I went cold on purpose and left his messages unanswered, just to see if he'd chase me. He usually did, for a while. Once, while he was in the shower, I opened his phone and scrolled through his chats. Nothing. And still I felt worse, not better, like a thief. My friend Rashmi said, "Hafsa, you're asking him to pass a test he doesn't know he's taking." She was right. Adil got quieter and more tired, and by May he said, "I feel like I'm always on trial." That sentence frightened me more than any imagined rival ever had.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do while Adil was in the shower?
qa.a: She opened his phone and scrolled through his chats.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after checking Adil's phone and finding nothing?
qa.a: She felt worse, not relieved, and guilty like a thief, because the test gave her no real reassurance.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done instead of setting tests?
qa.a: She could have told Adil plainly that she felt insecure and asked for reassurance, instead of provoking him to prove himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Adil to be tested without knowing it?
qa.a: Adil grew quiet and tired and felt he was always on trial, which wore down the closeness Hafsa was trying to protect.

grounding: Shows a young woman testing her partner with half-joking remarks, pulling away and checking his phone, and how it wears them both down.

passage:
Monday. Binita asked Raghav, for the third time that week, who he had been texting at lunch. "My project partner," he said, and showed her. She nodded, but didn't smile. He walked to class feeling like a suspect.
Thursday. Raghav turned his phone face down on the café table before she arrived. He hadn't done anything. He just wanted one small corner of his life that wasn't checked. When Binita noticed, her eyes narrowed. "Why's it upside down?"
"Because I'm tired of explaining," he snapped, and regretted the tone at once.
The next Sunday. He had put a lock on the phone and stopped mentioning his evening football. Binita said quietly, "You're hiding things now. I knew it."
Raghav stared at her. "I'm hiding because you keep searching."
Both of them felt completely right, and neither moved.

qa.q: What did Raghav do with his phone on Thursday before Binita arrived?
qa.a: He turned his phone face down on the café table.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he snapped, 'Because I'm tired of explaining'?
qa.a: He felt resentful and worn out from being treated like a suspect, and then regretted his tone.

qa.q: What could interrupt this spiral at this stage?
qa.a: One of them could name the loop out loud, that his privacy is self-protection and her questions come from fear, and ask for a calm talk, perhaps with a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Binita read Raghav's new privacy?
qa.a: To Binita the phone lock and the missing football updates look like proof that he is hiding something, which feeds her fear.

grounding: Shows a young man who feels distrusted guarding more privacy, which Binita reads as hiding, so each person's protection confirms the other's story.

subtype: Stage 5: Owning the feeling without accusing [Response]
passage: Counselling centre, notes after a joint session. Madhuri came in with Nitin today, at her own request. In our last meeting she had described checking his location and then feeling ashamed. Today she had practised a sentence, and she said it slowly, looking at him, not at me: "I feel insecure when you go quiet after parties, and I know it's mine to work on. I'd like some reassurance, but I won't ask for proof anymore." Nitin's shoulders dropped. He said, "I didn't know it was that. I thought you thought I was lying." He offered to text when he is leaving a party, and she said that would help. The tone in the room changed completely; for the first time in our sessions they sat like two people on the same side. I suggested Madhuri continue individual sessions on her self-worth, and she agreed. Next appointment Friday.

qa.q: What did Nitin offer to do?
qa.a: He offered to text when he is leaving a party.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have felt while saying her practised sentence?
qa.a: She was probably nervous but determined, having felt ashamed about checking his location and now choosing to own her insecurity without blaming him.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's sentence change the tone in the room?
qa.a: By owning the feeling and asking for reassurance without demanding proof, she invited Nitin to care for her rather than defend himself.

qa.q: How does Nitin experience Madhuri's words?
qa.a: Nitin feels relieved, his shoulders dropping, because he had believed she thought he was lying and now understands it is insecurity.

grounding: Shows a young woman naming her insecurity as her own and asking for reassurance without demanding proof, and the care this invites.

passage:
Santosh,
It's been a year, and I wanted to write this down instead of saying it badly over dinner.
Six months ago I was the girlfriend who counted your replies. You never once made me feel foolish for it. You kept telling me where you were before I asked, and you introduced me to everyone at your office party, which I know you did on purpose.
But your openness couldn't fix the part of me that felt not enough. That part I had to work on myself. The Thursday sessions with the college counsellor helped more than I expected. So did pottery on Sundays, and getting back in touch with Shalu and the old hostel group.
Last week you went on the office trip and I didn't check anything. I just missed you. That felt new, and good.
Ira

qa.q: What does Ira do on Sundays now?
qa.a: Ira does pottery on Sundays.

qa.q: How did Ira feel during Santosh's office trip last week?
qa.a: Ira felt secure enough not to check anything and simply missed Santosh, which felt new and calm.

qa.q: Which steps helped Ira build inner security?
qa.a: Thursday sessions with the college counsellor, pottery, and reconnecting with Shalu and the hostel group, alongside Santosh being open and consistent.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Santosh during the months when Ira counted replies?
qa.a: Santosh may have felt watched at times, yet chose patience, sharing plans before being asked and including Ira at the office party.

grounding: Shows a young woman building her own worth through friends, interests and a counsellor while her partner stays open and consistent.

subtype: Stage 1: The juicy piece of news [Actor]
passage:
On Tuesday, Elif was sent to the school office in Copenhagen with the class register. Outside the door sat Freja from her class, crying into her sleeve. Through the half-open door Elif heard the secretary say, "...her father has moved out, so her mother will collect her from now on..."
Elif walked back slowly, her heart thumping. Nobody else knew. Just her. She felt taller somehow, as if she were carrying something heavy and shiny.
At the coat hooks, Lars asked, "What took you so long?"
Elif's mouth opened. The words were right there, bursting to get out. "I know something," she whispered, eyes wide. "Something big about Freja."

qa.q: Who was crying outside the school office?
qa.a: Freja from Elif's class was crying into her sleeve outside the door.

qa.q: How did Elif feel as she walked back knowing something nobody else knew?
qa.a: She felt important and excited, as if she were carrying something heavy and shiny, and she was eager to tell.

qa.q: What could Elif do at the coat hooks instead of telling Lars?
qa.a: She could keep what she overheard to herself, or quietly ask a teacher whether Freja is okay, because it is Freja's private family business.

qa.q: If you were Freja, what would you want Elif to do with what she heard?
qa.a: Freja would probably want it kept private, and maybe a kind word, not whispers at the coat hooks.

grounding: Shows a child who overhears a fragment about a crying classmate's family and feels important and eager to tell.

passage:
During the lunch break at their Bhopal school, Indu pulled Abhinav behind the water cooler. "You're my best friend, so I'll tell only you," she said. "Yesterday I saw Shabnam's mother shouting at her near the gate."
That part was true. Indu had seen a woman speaking loudly, and Shabnam staring at her shoes.
"And," Indu went on, lowering her voice, "I think she's going to be sent to another school."
Abhinav's eyes went round. "Really?"
"Really," said Indu. As she said it, it sounded real even to her. Nobody had mentioned another school. But the story felt better with that part in, and Abhinav was listening so hard.

qa.q: Where did Indu pull Abhinav during the lunch break?
qa.a: She pulled him behind the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Indu add the part about another school?
qa.a: She enjoyed feeling important and wanted the story to sound more exciting, and the guess began to feel true even to her.

qa.q: What could Indu do before adding to a story next time?
qa.a: She could ask herself, 'Did I see this or am I guessing?' and leave out anything she only imagined, or not share it at all.

qa.q: How might Shabnam feel if she heard this version of the story?
qa.a: Shabnam would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, since the story adds something that never happened.

grounding: Shows a child telling her best friend what she saw and adding a guessed detail that soon sounds true.

passage:
In Class 5B of a Delhi school, the story travelled from desk to desk like a folded chit. "Don't tell anyone," Dolma whispered to Pranav during art, "but Ritesh failed and has to repeat the year."
Pranav nodded. He watched it move: Dolma told the twins, the twins told Aman, and every telling began with "promise you won't say". Pranav noticed that the whisperers leaned together like a club. He had never been in that club.
At recess, when Aman and the twins huddled near the swings, Pranav walked up and said, "I heard it too. About Ritesh."
They made room for him at once. He felt warm, included, and a little sick, all at the same time.

qa.q: How did every telling of the story begin?
qa.a: Every telling began with "promise you won't say".

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the group made room for him?
qa.a: He felt warm and included, and at the same time a little sick, because he had joined in by repeating the story.

qa.q: What could Pranav have done at the swings instead of repeating the story?
qa.a: He could have joined the group with something else to talk about, or said he didn't want to pass it on, since belonging does not have to cost Ritesh.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritesh while the whisper travels around 5B?
qa.a: Ritesh may notice huddles and glances without knowing why, and feel uneasy or left out as the story grows behind his back.

grounding: Shows a whispered story spreading with promises of secrecy, and a listener repeating it to feel part of the group.

passage:
On the bus home from school near Nashik, Reena saw two classmates look at her and giggle behind their hands. All day, whispering had stopped whenever she came near. Finally Indu said quietly, "They're saying your father went to jail, because of the police jeep at your house."
Reena's face burned. The jeep had come because someone stole their goat; her father had only given a statement. She wanted to jump off the bus and never go back. She also wanted to shove those girls off their seat. Her hands shook in her lap.
At home she would not eat. Aaji sat beside her on the charpai and asked gently, "Who hurt you today?" Reena told her everything. Aaji held her hand. "This is not your shame. Tomorrow I will come to school with you."

qa.q: Why had the police jeep come to Reena's house?
qa.a: It had come because someone stole their goat; her father had only given a statement.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when Indu told her what people were saying?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry, her face burning and hands shaking, wanting both to hide and to shove the girls.

qa.q: What helped Reena at this point, and what could come next?
qa.a: Aaji noticed, listened and told her it was not her shame; going to school together tomorrow can get the false story stopped by the teachers.

qa.q: What might Indu have been feeling when deciding to tell Reena?
qa.a: Indu may have felt uneasy and torn, wanting Reena to know what was being said even though it would hurt to hear.

grounding: Shows a girl noticing stares and giggles, learning a partly false story about her family, and feeling shame and anger.
